title: The boy who knew everything but this
hook: Shvetaketu comes home after twelve years of study, proud, and his father asks the one question he can't answer
carry: you are that: the self is never lost, only unseen

segments.voice: Yesterday, jnana and Shankara's preface: the I and the this, mixed up like silver seen on a shell.

In the Chandogya Upanishad, a boy named Shvetaketu leaves home at twelve to study the Vedas. He comes back at twenty-four, having learned them all, and he walks in proud, sure he knows everything. His father, Uddalaka, asks him one question. Did you ask for the teaching by which what hasn't been heard becomes heard, what hasn't been thought becomes thought, what isn't known becomes known? Shvetaketu has no idea what he means. So his father gives a clue: know one lump of clay, and you know everything made of clay; the pots are only names. Shvetaketu admits it. My teachers can't have known this, or they'd have told me. Please, sir, teach me. And lesson after lesson, his father ends on the same three words, usually rendered: you are that.
screen: `TWELVE YEARS OF STUDY.` → `ONE QUESTION HE CAN'T ANSWER.` → `YOU ARE THAT.`

segments.voice: Centuries later, Shankara opens his commentary on the Brahma Sutra with Shvetaketu's problem. The first line says: now, therefore, the wish to know Brahman. But is Brahman known already, or not? If known, why inquire? If wholly unknown, how could anyone even want it? His answer: Brahman is known, in a way, because it is the self of everyone. Nobody ever thinks, I am not. What's in doubt is what this self is. Some say the body, some the senses, some the mind, some a flicker of awareness, some a self that acts and enjoys. Shvetaketu was just like that: full of learning, unclear about the one thing closest to him. Shankara's own answer is the father's: the self, atman, is Brahman, the reality behind everything. That is the heart of Advaita Vedanta. So jnana isn't finding a new object. It's clarity about what was never missing. Other Vedanta schools honor the same three words and read them differently; Ramanuja, for one, hears in them the Lord as the inner self of every self. Today, plenty of people travel far to find themselves. This teaching turns the search around: the one looking is what's being looked for.
screen: `KNOWN, OR UNKNOWN?` · `NOBODY THINKS: I AM NOT.` · `ATMAN IS BRAHMAN.` · `THE ONE LOOKING IS THE ONE LOOKED FOR.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and ask, quietly, the question many Advaita teachers give, made famous by Ramana Maharshi: who am I? Let the mind offer its answers, this body, these feelings, these thoughts, and let each one pass without deciding. Come back each time to the plain sense of being here, before any label. If you pray, offer that plain presence; if you don't, simply rest in it.
Jnana. Knowing. On Shankara's reading of the first line, not finding something new, but becoming clear about a self that is never lacking.
Your line: you are that: the self is never lost, only unseen. Shvetaketu knew everything but this. I'll be here tomorrow.

howItsDone: In Advaita Vedanta, students hear the Upanishads' great sayings, such as you are that, from a teacher, reflect on them, and sit with the question of what the self is; Shankara's commentary on the first sutra is a classic place to begin.

original.note: Sanskrit: the wish to know, from the same root as jnana; the key word of the Brahma Sutra's first line.

Shvetaketu.meaning: Uddalaka's son, who came home proud after twelve years of study

Uddalaka.meaning: the sage who taught his son 'you are that'

Brahman.meaning: the ultimate reality, ground of all

Brahma Sutra.meaning: tiny, packed lines summing up the Upanishads' teaching

jnana.meaning: knowing, and the way of freedom through knowing

Vedanta.meaning: the schools that read the Upanishads and the Brahma Sutras

notes: Paraphrase of Shankara on 1.1.1: the known/unknown dilemma; the existence of Brahman known as the self of all ('everyone is conscious that the self exists, and never thinks I am not'); the list of views (body with intelligence, the senses, the internal organ, momentary cognition, the void, an agent and enjoyer, an enjoyer only, an omniscient Lord, the self of the enjoyer).
